metadata.title: Induction of Decision Trees
metadata.source_note: Extracted from PDF->text fallback; .tex source not available. Math fidelity reduced.

nodes.name: Universe of objects and attributes
nodes.statement: The basis of the induction task is a universe of objects described by a collection of attributes; each attribute takes a small set of discrete, mutually exclusive values.
nodes.statement_clean: Objects are described by a fixed set of discrete-valued attributes.

nodes.name: Class (P and N)
nodes.statement: Each object belongs to one of mutually exclusive classes; for the two-class treatment they are denoted $P$ (positive) and $N$ (negative).
nodes.statement_clean: Each object has a class label, restricted here to two values P and N.

nodes.name: Training set
nodes.statement: A training set is a collection of objects whose classes are known; the induction task is to develop a classification rule from it that determines the class of any object from its attribute values.
nodes.statement_clean: Training set: objects with known classes used as input to induction.

nodes.name: Adequate attributes
nodes.statement: Attributes are inadequate for a training set if it contains two objects with identical attribute values but different classes; otherwise they are adequate.
nodes.statement_clean: Attributes are adequate iff no two same-attribute objects have different classes.

nodes.name: Decision tree
nodes.statement: A decision tree is a tree whose leaves are class names and whose internal nodes are attribute-based tests with one branch per outcome; classification proceeds from the root by evaluating tests until a leaf is reached.
nodes.statement_clean: Decision tree: leaves give classes; internal nodes test attributes.

nodes.name: Window (in iterative ID3)
nodes.statement: The window is a subset of the training set, chosen at random, on which an initial decision tree is grown; misclassified objects are added on subsequent iterations.
nodes.statement_clean: Window: random subset of training data driving each ID3 iteration.

nodes.name: Noise
nodes.statement: Non-systematic errors in the values of attributes or in the class information of training objects are referred to as noise.
nodes.statement_clean: Noise: random errors in attribute values or class labels.

nodes.name: Predictive accuracy
nodes.statement: Predictive accuracy is the rate at which the induced decision tree correctly classifies objects outside the training set.
nodes.statement_clean: Predictive accuracy: classification accuracy on unseen objects.

nodes.name: Token (for unknown-value classification)
nodes.statement: When classifying an object with unknown attribute values, a token of value $T$ is passed; on a test of attribute $A$ each branch $i$ receives a token of value $T \cdot \mathrm{ratio}_i$, distributing weight in proportion to the relative frequency of values.
nodes.statement_clean: Token: a fractional weight propagated down branches when an attribute value is unknown.

nodes.name: Information needed to classify (entropy)
nodes.statement: $I(p,n) = -\frac{p}{p+n}\log_2\frac{p}{p+n} - \frac{n}{p+n}\log_2\frac{n}{p+n}$.
nodes.statement_clean: Binary entropy of the class distribution in a node.

nodes.name: Expected information after testing attribute A
nodes.statement: $E(A) = \sum_{i=1}^{v} \frac{p_i + n_i}{p+n}\, I(p_i, n_i)$, the weighted average of subset entropies after branching on attribute $A$.
nodes.statement_clean: Weighted average entropy of children produced by attribute A.

nodes.name: Information gain
nodes.statement: $\mathrm{gain}(A) = I(p,n) - E(A)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Information gain of attribute A: entropy reduction from branching on A.

nodes.name: Chi-square statistic for attribute relevance
nodes.statement: $\sum_{i=1}^{v}\frac{(p_i - p'_i)^2}{p'_i} + \frac{(n_i - n'_i)^2}{n'_i}$ where $p'_i = p\cdot(p_i+n_i)/(p+n)$ and similarly for $n'_i$; approximately $\chi^2$ with $v-1$ degrees of freedom under independence.
nodes.statement_clean: Chi-square test statistic for whether attribute A is independent of the class.

nodes.name: Unknown-value reweighting
nodes.statement: Effective count $p_i + p_u\cdot\mathrm{ratio}_i$ where $\mathrm{ratio}_i = (p_i+n_i)/\sum_i (p_i+n_i)$; unknown-valued objects are distributed across known values in proportion to their relative frequency.
nodes.statement_clean: Distribute unknown-valued objects across branches in proportion to known-value frequencies.

nodes.name: Information value of an attribute
nodes.statement: $\mathrm{IV}(A) = -\sum_{i=1}^{v}\frac{p_i+n_i}{p+n}\log_2\frac{p_i+n_i}{p+n}$, the information content of the answer to 'what is the value of $A$?'.
nodes.statement_clean: Entropy of the marginal distribution of attribute A's values.

nodes.name: Gain ratio
nodes.statement: $\mathrm{gain\_ratio}(A) = \mathrm{gain}(A) / \mathrm{IV}(A)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Ratio of information gain to attribute information value.

nodes.name: Expected error of probabilistic-leaf classification
nodes.statement: If a leaf classifies an object as $P$ with probability $p/(p+n)$, the expected error on similarly distributed objects is $\frac{2pn}{(p+n)^2}$.
nodes.statement_clean: Expected error when leaf class is sampled in proportion to p:n.

nodes.name: Decision-tree induction task
nodes.statement: Given a training set of objects with known classes and discrete-valued attributes, develop a decision tree that classifies any object (in or outside the training set) from its attribute values.
nodes.statement_clean: Induce a classifier in decision-tree form from labelled training data.

nodes.name: Choosing the test attribute at each node
nodes.statement: At each non-leaf node, choose an attribute on which to branch so that the resulting decision tree is simple and accurate.
nodes.statement_clean: How to pick the splitting attribute at each tree node.

nodes.name: Inducing decision trees from noisy training sets
nodes.statement: Adapt the tree-building algorithm to operate when attribute values or class labels in the training set may be corrupted by noise.
nodes.statement_clean: Build accurate decision trees despite noisy training data.

nodes.name: Handling unknown attribute values
nodes.statement: Build and use decision trees when some attribute values are missing in the training set or in objects to be classified.
nodes.statement_clean: Handle missing attribute values in training and classification.

nodes.name: Multi-valued attribute bias of the gain criterion
nodes.statement: The information-gain criterion tends to favour attributes with many values, so an alternative selection criterion is needed that does not exhibit this bias.
nodes.statement_clean: Avoid the gain criterion's bias toward many-valued attributes.

nodes.name: CLS (Concept Learning System)
nodes.statement: Builds a decision tree by limited-depth lookahead minimising a weighted measurement+misclassification cost; the precursor of ID3.
input: Set of training objects with cost structure
output: Decision tree minimising expected cost in the lookahead-limited search

nodes.name: Divide-and-conquer tree construction
nodes.statement: If $C$ is empty or single-class, return a leaf; otherwise pick a test $T$ with outcomes $O_1,\dots,O_w$, partition $C$ into $\{C_1,\dots,C_w\}$, and recursively build subtrees for each $C_i$.
output: Decision tree correctly classifying every object in $C$

nodes.name: ID3
nodes.statement: Top-down decision-tree learner: an iterative outer loop grows the tree on a window of the training set, choosing at each node the attribute maximising information gain $\mathrm{gain}(A) = I(p,n) - E(A)$.
input: Training set with discrete-valued attributes and two classes $P, N$
output: Decision tree classifying all training objects

nodes.name: ACLS
nodes.statement: Generalisation of ID3 that additionally permits attributes with unrestricted integer values.
input: Training set with discrete and integer-valued attributes
output: Decision tree using thresholded integer attributes

nodes.name: ASSISTANT
nodes.statement: ID3 descendant that handles continuous attributes, hierarchical classes, and uses binary tests via a value-subset selection criterion.
input: Training set with discrete, integer, or continuous attributes; possibly hierarchical classes

nodes.name: Chi-square pre-pruning
nodes.statement: Before splitting on attribute $A$, compute the $\chi^2$ statistic for independence of $A$ from the class; do not split unless independence can be rejected at high confidence (e.g. 99%).
output: Decision: split on $A$ or stop and form a leaf

nodes.name: Majority-class leaf assignment
nodes.statement: When testing must stop on a mixed collection $C$, label the leaf with class $P$ if $p>n$, with $N$ if $p<n$, and with either if $p=n$ (minimises sum of absolute errors).
input: Mixed-class collection $C$ with $p$ class-$P$ and $n$ class-$N$ objects

nodes.name: Unknown-value handling at training time
nodes.statement: When evaluating $\mathrm{gain}(A)$, distribute objects with unknown $A$ across known values in proportion to relative frequency $\mathrm{ratio}_i$; once $A$ is chosen, discard unknown-valued objects when forming subtrees.
input: Collection $C$ with some objects having unknown values of $A$
output: Adjusted gain estimate, then subtrees over known-valued subsets

nodes.name: Token-based classification with unknown values
nodes.statement: Pass a token of value $T$ down the tree; at each test on an attribute whose value is unknown, split the token across branches in proportion to $\mathrm{ratio}_i$; sum token weights at leaves per class and pick the class with the highest total.
input: Object whose value of some attribute is unknown
output: Class label (and optional confidence) assigned to the object

nodes.name: Subset (binary) selection criterion
nodes.statement: For attribute $A$ with values $A_1,\dots,A_v$ choose a subset $S$; the test has two branches (in $S$ vs not in $S$); the chosen $(A,S)$ maximises information gain.
output: Binary test based on a subset of attribute values

nodes.name: Gain-ratio selection criterion
nodes.statement: Among attributes with average-or-better $\mathrm{gain}(A)$, choose the one maximising $\mathrm{gain}(A)/\mathrm{IV}(A)$.

nodes.name: Continuous-attribute thresholding
nodes.statement: Sort distinct values $V_1,\dots,V_k$ of a continuous attribute $A$ and consider thresholds $(V_i+V_{i+1})/2$, evaluating information gain of the resulting binary split.
input: Continuous attribute $A$ with sorted distinct values
output: Best threshold and associated binary split

nodes.name: Bayesian unknown-value imputation
nodes.statement: Estimate $\Pr(A=A_i\mid \mathrm{class}=P) = p_i/p$ from objects with known values; replace unknown value by the most likely $A_i$ or by fractional copies weighted by these probabilities.
output: Imputed value or fractional-object distribution for $A$

nodes.name: Decision-tree-based unknown-value imputation
nodes.statement: Treat the value of $A$ as the class and the original class as another attribute; build a decision tree on $C'$ (objects with $A$ defined) and use it to fill in $A$ for the rest.
output: Imputed value of $A$ for each object in $C-C'$

nodes.name: Splitting an attribute value never decreases information gain
nodes.statement: Let $A'$ be obtained from $A$ by splitting one value into two. Then $\mathrm{gain}(A') \ge \mathrm{gain}(A)$, with equality only when the class proportions are the same in both subdivisions.
assumptions: $A$ is a discrete-valued attribute on training set $C$
$A'$ refines $A$ by splitting a single value
conclusions: $\mathrm{gain}(A') \ge \mathrm{gain}(A)$, equal only when class proportions match across the split

nodes.name: Unknown-reweighting only decreases gain
nodes.statement: The reweighting $p_i \to p_i + p_u\cdot\mathrm{ratio}_i$ has the property that unknown values can only decrease the information gain of an attribute.
assumptions: Unknown-valued objects are redistributed by the ratio formula in EP203.5
conclusions: $\mathrm{gain}(A)$ computed with unknown reweighting is $\le$ the gain over known-valued objects only

nodes.name: Iterative ID3 may fail to converge if window is bounded
nodes.statement: The iterative window-based ID3 framework cannot be guaranteed to converge on a final tree unless the window can grow to include the entire training set.
conclusions: No convergence guarantee on a final decision tree

nodes.name: Computational complexity per node
nodes.statement: At each non-leaf node ID3 has computational cost $O(|C|\cdot|A|)$ where $|C|$ is the size of the collection and $|A|$ is the number of attributes; total cost per iteration is proportional to training-set size $\times$ number of attributes $\times$ number of non-leaf nodes.
assumptions: Each gain evaluation scans every object once per attribute
conclusions: No exponential growth has been observed empirically as task size increases

nodes.name: Simpler trees generalise better (Occam preference)
nodes.statement: Given two decision trees correct on the training set, the simpler one is more likely to capture the inherent structure and so to classify unseen objects correctly; upper bounds on expected error grow with the complexity of the induced generalisation.
assumptions: Training set of fixed predetermined size
Two decision trees, both consistent with the training set
conclusions: Prefer the simpler tree; expected-error bounds increase with hypothesis complexity

nodes.name: Saturday morning weather (Table 1)
nodes.statement: Fourteen training objects described by attributes outlook $\in\{$sunny, overcast, rain$\}$, temperature $\in\{$cool, mild, hot$\}$, humidity $\in\{$high, normal$\}$, windy $\in\{$true, false$\}$, with class $P$ or $N$.

nodes.name: ID3 gain computation on Saturday-morning data
nodes.statement: On the Table 1 data: $I(p,n)=0.940$ bits; $E(\text{outlook})=0.694$, so $\mathrm{gain}(\text{outlook})=0.246$, vs $0.029$ (temperature), $0.151$ (humidity), $0.048$ (windy); ID3 selects outlook for the root.

nodes.name: Gain-ratio computation on Saturday-morning data
nodes.statement: Only outlook and humidity have above-average gain; $\mathrm{IV}(\text{outlook})=1.578$, $\mathrm{IV}(\text{humidity})=1$; gain-ratio is $0.156$ vs $0.151$, so outlook is still chosen but its margin shrinks.

nodes.name: Chess-endgame induction (KRKN)
nodes.statement: $1.4$ million chess positions with $49$ binary attributes reduce to $715$ distinct objects (correct tree $\sim 150$ nodes); training on a random 20% gave decision trees classifying over $84\%$ of unseen objects correctly.

nodes.name: Noise corruption study (Table 2)
nodes.statement: On the 551-object 39-attribute task, noise levels 5%-100% are applied to a single attribute, all attributes, or class labels; class noise gives roughly linear error growth, all-attribute noise rises rapidly then declines as the chi-square cutoff fires.

nodes.name: Unknown attribute-value imputation comparison (Table 3)
nodes.statement: For the three most important attributes, decision-tree imputation fails 19-22% of the time, vs 27-38% for Bayesian and 27-40% for most-common-value imputation.

nodes.name: Unknown-value classification degradation (Figure 5)
nodes.statement: On the 551-object 39-attribute task, decision-tree training and classification under various ignorance levels degrades gracefully; even at 10% ignorance about 90% of unknown-bearing objects are still classified correctly.

nodes.name: Anomaly of treating 'unknown' as a separate value
nodes.statement: For a balanced attribute $A$ with $E(A)=1$ bit, replacing one $A_1$ object's value by 'unknown' yields $A'$ with $E(A')=0.84$ bits, so $A'$ appears to gain more information than $A$ - opposite to common sense.

nodes.name: Maximising gain equivalent to minimising E(A)
nodes.statement: Since $I(p,n)$ is constant across attributes, maximising $\mathrm{gain}(A)$ is equivalent to minimising $E(A)$, the mutual information of attribute $A$ with the class.

nodes.name: ASSISTANT uses an information-based pruning measure
nodes.statement: ASSISTANT uses an information-based measure to perform much the same noise-pruning function as the chi-square test, but no comparative results were available at publication.

nodes.name: Counter-productive to denoise training only
nodes.statement: At higher noise levels, a correct tree from clean training data classified noisy field data worse than a tree trained on similarly noisy data; eliminating noise only at training time can be counter-productive.

nodes.name: Subset criterion may be infeasible for many-valued attributes
nodes.statement: An attribute with $v$ values has $2^{v-1}-1$ non-trivial subsets, so the subset criterion is roughly $2^{v-1}-1$ times more expensive than a binary attribute; infeasible for $v\approx 20$.

nodes.name: Hart's chi-square selection criterion
nodes.statement: Hart proposed using the chi-square confidence level itself as the selection criterion (pick the attribute with highest confidence of class-dependence); the test is valid only when expected counts $p'_i, n'_i$ exceed about four.

nodes.name: Structured Induction
nodes.statement: Shapiro's Structured Induction approach decomposes an opaque large decision tree into a hierarchy of small trees over notional super-attributes, recovering intelligibility for domain experts.

nodes.name: Multi-tree (per-class) classification
nodes.statement: Instead of one multi-class tree, build one tree per class (e.g. monkey-vs-not, giraffe-vs-not); Shoppers argues this gives more accurate classification of unseen objects, at the cost of needing tie-breaking when multiple or no trees match.

nodes.name: Derivation of the high-noise expected-error decline
nodes.statement: Show that the peak-and-decline shape of error under all-attribute noise follows from comparing the expected error of probabilistic-leaf classification ($2pn/(p+n)^2$) with majority-class classification ($n/(p+n)$ when $p>n$).
